title: Optimization of Deep Learning Model for Denoising Dose Profiles in Proton Therapy
summary:
Proton therapy offers a dosimetric advantage over conventional radiotherapy through the Bragg peak, enabling precise dose delivery to the tumour while sparing surrounding tissue. Monte Carlo (MC) simulation provides the most accurate dose calculation but is computationally expensive for clinical workflows. A promising compromise is to simulate with a reduced number of primary histories and recover a high-quality dose distribution through a deep learning denoising step.
  In this work, we take a 3D multiscale U-Net from recent literature as a case study and investigate two improvements critical for clinical deployment. First, we replace the standard MSE training objective with a differentiable $γ$-index-based loss, extended to native 3D operation, and demonstrate that directly optimising the clinical evaluation metric yields a mean Gamma Passing Rate of 99.47\% at 2mm/2\% and 95.67\% at 1mm/1\% on the test set, compared to 92.10\% and 71.13\% for MSE. Second, we apply L1-norm structured filter pruning to reduce the model's memory footprint, achieving a 13.3\% parameter reduction with negligible performance loss under partial pruning, and 20\% reduction under full-block pruning after fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: This work improves a 3D multiscale U-Net for denoising low-statistics Monte Carlo proton therapy dose distributions by (1) replacing MSE with a differentiable native 3D gamma-index loss and (2) applying L1-norm structured filter pruning.
AI.motivation: Monte Carlo dose calculation is the most accurate but too slow for clinical proton therapy workflows. Simulating fewer primary histories and recovering quality via deep learning denoising is a promising compromise, but clinical deployment requires optimization for the actual clinical metric and reduced memory footprint.
AI.method: Using a recent 3D multiscale U-Net as a case study, the authors (1) replace the MSE training objective with a differentiable gamma-index-based loss extended to native 3D operation, and (2) apply L1-norm structured filter pruning to shrink the model.
AI.result: The gamma loss achieves Gamma Passing Rates of 99.47% at 2mm/2% and 95.67% at 1mm/1%, versus 92.10% and 71.13% for MSE. Pruning yields 13.3% parameter reduction with negligible loss under partial pruning, and 20% under full-block pruning after fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Directly optimizing the clinical evaluation metric and pruning filters both improve the practicality of deep learning denoising for proton therapy dose calculation, enabling better accuracy and lower memory cost for clinical deployment.

title: Dynamical Insights into the Current Control Strategies for Chikungunya
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures Accepted by SCIENTIA SINICA Mathematica (in Chinese)
summary: This paper addresses the challenge that, under China's current mosquito-control policy for chikungunya---\textit{clearing stagnant water, killing adult mosquitoes, and preventing bites}---epidemics can still recur and continue to rise. By constructing a vector--host dynamical model that incorporates asymptomatic infections and a screening rate, we derive approximate analytical expressions for the epidemic peak value and peak time, and reveal the intrinsic link between short-term transients and long-term outcomes. Simulations across three scenarios---human-seeded, mosquito-seeded, and joint human--mosquito-seeded---show that (i) even when the vector population is effectively suppressed, asymptomatic carriers can still sustain transmission; (ii) the effect of the screening rate on the peak time is non-monotonic, and there exists a critical threshold that maximizes the delay of the epidemic; and (iii) moderate screening can both suppress the first wave and avoid leaving an excessively large susceptible pool that would amplify subsequent waves. Accordingly, we upgrade the original policy to a \textit{Twelve-character} strategy for prevention, mitigation, and control---\textit{clearing stagnant water, killing adult mosquitoes, preventing bites, and screening cases early}---providing theoretical support for chikungunya and other mosquito-borne diseases.

AI.tldr: A vector-host model with asymptomatic infection and screening shows China's chikungunya control policy can be improved by adding early case screening, proposing a "Twelve-character" strategy.
AI.motivation: Under China's current chikungunya policy (clearing stagnant water, killing adult mosquitoes, preventing bites), epidemics can still recur and rise, so better control guidance is needed.
AI.method: Construct a vector-host dynamical model incorporating asymptomatic infections and a screening rate; derive approximate analytical expressions for epidemic peak value and peak time; run simulations under human-seeded, mosquito-seeded, and joint seeding scenarios.
AI.result: Asymptomatic carriers sustain transmission even when vectors are suppressed; screening rate non-monotonically affects peak time with a critical threshold maximizing delay; moderate screening suppresses the first wave without leaving a large susceptible pool that amplifies later waves.
AI.conclusion: The policy is upgraded to a "Twelve-character" strategy: clearing stagnant water, killing adult mosquitoes, preventing bites, and screening cases early, offering theoretical support for chikungunya and other mosquito-borne diseases.

title: A Shortcut to Structure in AlphaFold 3
summary: AlphaFold 3 predicts protein structures with remarkable accuracy, yet how structural information emerges within the model remains poorly understood. Here, through causal interventions on internal representations and direct probing of every Pairformer block, we trace the formation of global protein geometry and identify the multiple sequence alignment (MSA) as a structural shortcut to the fold. Removing the MSA largely preserves local secondary structure while disrupting the long-range relationships that define global topology. Restoring the MSA-enriched pair representation at only forty residues recovers most of this lost organization, including at pairs never directly modified. This contribution depends on the detailed direction of the MSA module's output rather than its magnitude. The Pairformer rapidly converts this signal into global geometry: the final fold becomes recoverable by approximately block 9 of 48 for a majority of proteins, roughly twenty-seven blocks before the model's decoder can render it, whereas without the MSA it remains inaccessible for most proteins throughout the pass. Which homologs are supplied shapes this trajectory more strongly than which query is supplied; it persists for a designed query that never evolved but collapses for a shuffled sequence. Most importantly, an alignment built for a different protein that shares the fold, supplied only at the structurally corresponding columns, raises the median TM-score against experiment from 0.44 to 0.72, while the same alignment shifted a few residues along the chain performs worse than supplying no alignment at all. What AlphaFold 3 reads from an alignment is therefore a description of the fold itself, transferable between proteins that share one, rather than the query's own evolutionary history. This explains both its accuracy and the limits of what it has solved.

AI.tldr: Through causal interventions and probing of AlphaFold 3's Pairformer blocks, the MSA is shown to act as a transferable structural shortcut: it encodes the fold itself rather than the query's evolutionary history, and the Pairformer converts this signal into global geometry within ~9 of 48 blocks.
AI.motivation: AlphaFold 3 predicts structures accurately, but how structural information emerges internally is poorly understood. The authors aim to mechanistically trace where and how global protein geometry forms, and to clarify what the model actually reads from an MSA.
AI.method: Causal interventions on internal representations and direct probing of every Pairformer block; ablating MSA; partially restoring MSA-enriched pair representations at only 40 residues; swapping in alignments from homologous proteins; shuffling sequences; and testing column-shifted alignments.
AI.result: Removing MSA preserves local secondary structure but disrupts long-range topology; restoring MSA signal at just 40 residues recovers most global organization (direction matters more than magnitude). Final fold is recoverable by ~block 9 of 48 for most proteins, ~27 blocks before the decoder can render it, but stays inaccessible without MSA. Homolog choice matters more than query choice. A fold-sharing alignment from a different protein raises median TM-score from 0.44 to 0.72, while a column-shifted version performs worse than no alignment.
AI.conclusion: AlphaFold 3 reads an alignment as a description of the fold itself—transferable between proteins sharing that fold—rather than the query's own evolutionary history. This accounts for both its accuracy and the limits of what it has solved.

title: Beyond the Transcriptome: Chromatin-Informed Prediction of Cell-State-Dependent Perturbation Responses
summary: Predicting transcriptional responses to genetic perturbations is central to understanding gene function. Existing predictors primarily rely on transcriptomic measurements, although chromatin accessibility provides complementary information about the cellular context in which perturbations act. Using this information requires linking chromatin context to specific perturbations and accounting for baseline differences between independently sampled control and perturbed populations. We propose ChromaPert, a chromatin-informed framework for predicting state-dependent perturbation responses. ChromaPert combines molecular and DNA-informed locus priors with paired control RNA--ATAC features to jointly represent target identity and measured cellular context. Its Chromatin-Guided Response Router (CGRR) builds a source bank of control-derived expression offsets and retrieves relevant sources using perturbation/locus or control-ATAC similarity. These offsets account for baseline differences, while conditional transport flow learns the remaining response. Across three unseen-target and held-out-state settings on K562 CAT-ATAC and Perturb-Multiome, ChromaPert achieves the highest all-gene response correlation among evaluated methods. When transferring known perturbations to held-out states, it improves correlation by 23.2% across all genes and 46.2% for the twenty most responsive genes over the strongest respective baselines. Correct RNA--ATAC pairing improves recovery of chromatin-associated response slopes over shuffled pairing, while cross-state predictions retain state-specific responses to the same perturbation.

AI.tldr: ChromaPert is a chromatin-informed framework that predicts state-dependent transcriptional responses to genetic perturbations by combining locus priors, paired control RNA-ATAC features, and a Chromatin-Guided Response Router.
AI.motivation: Existing perturbation-response predictors rely mainly on transcriptomics, ignoring chromatin accessibility that provides complementary cellular-context information. Using chromatin data requires linking chromatin context to perturbations and correcting baseline differences between independently sampled control and perturbed populations.
AI.method: ChromaPert jointly represents target identity and cellular context via molecular and DNA-informed locus priors plus paired control RNA-ATAC features. Its Chromatin-Guided Response Router (CGRR) builds a source bank of control-derived expression offsets, retrieved by perturbation/locus or control-ATAC similarity, to account for baseline differences, while conditional transport flow learns the residual response.
AI.result: On K562 CAT-ATAC and Perturb-Multiome across three unseen-target and held-out-state settings, ChromaPert achieves the highest all-gene response correlation. In transfer to held-out states it improves correlation by 23.2% (all genes) and 46.2% (top-20 responsive genes) over strongest baselines. Correct RNA-ATAC pairing improves chromatin-associated response-slope recovery over shuffled pairing, and cross-state predictions retain state-specific responses.
AI.conclusion: Chromatin context, properly paired and routed, enables more accurate and state-aware prediction of perturbation responses, outperforming transcriptome-only methods.

title: Scaling subjects in cross-modal alignment: video decoding with EEG foundation model
summary: Naturalistic visual decoding from EEG has long been constrained by cohort size: existing scaling literature caps out at a few dozen subjects, leading prior work to conclude that scaling subject cohorts yields minimal performance gains. Training a cross-modal EEG--video contrastive encoder on a cohort larger by more than an order of magnitude, we find the axis is productive but has an onset. Below $S\approx50$ --- the entirety of the range prior work occupies --- no model improves meaningfully over an untrained encoder; above it, decoding rises log-linearly in subject count with no saturation at the top of our ladder, on a fitted stimulus-feature probe and on fit-free movie-moment retrieval alike, and the gain transfers to a second, unseen film. How far the axis carries then depends on initialisation more than on capacity: an encoder initialised from an EEG foundation model scales ${\sim}1.6\times$ faster per doubling of the cohort than randomly initialised encoders at two depths, is the only one still converting subjects into retrieval accuracy at the top of the ladder, and converges on a fraction of the alignment compute. Subject scaling on shared naturalistic stimuli is thus an effective and currently unsaturated frontier for scaling EEG foundation models.

AI.tldr: Scaling the subject cohort for EEG-to-video decoding is productive but has an onset (~50 subjects); beyond it, decoding improves log-linearly without saturation, and EEG-foundation-model initialization scales ~1.6x faster per doubling.
AI.motivation: Prior scaling work on naturalistic EEG decoding maxes out at a few dozen subjects, concluding that enlarging subject cohorts yields little gain. The authors suspect this conclusion stems from operating entirely below a critical threshold.
AI.method: Train a cross-modal EEG--video contrastive encoder on a cohort an order of magnitude larger than prior work (>few hundred subjects). Evaluate on a fitted stimulus-feature probe and fit-free movie-moment retrieval, plus transfer to an unseen film, comparing random vs. EEG-foundation-model initialization at two depths.
AI.result: Below S≈50 subjects, no model beats an untrained encoder; above it, decoding rises log-linearly with subject count, with no saturation at the top of the ladder, and transfers to a second unseen film. The foundation-model-initialized encoder scales ~1.6x faster per doubling, is the only one still converting subjects into retrieval accuracy at the top, and converges on a fraction of the alignment compute.
AI.conclusion: Subject scaling on shared naturalistic stimuli is an effective, currently unsaturated frontier for scaling EEG foundation models, with initialization mattering more than capacity.

title: FaceKit: a Toolkit for Interpretable Facial Phenotyping, Synthetic Image Generation and Privacy Analysis in Rare Diseases
summary: Many rare genetic diseases are associated with recognizable craniofacial features. However, traditional approaches for describing facial morphology rely largely on qualitative clinical observation and free-text descriptions, which are often subjective, non-standardized, and difficult to reproduce across observers and institutions. Although the Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) provides controlled terms for describing facial features, these terms are typically categorical rather than quantitative and may vary depending on examiner experience and interpretation. Here, we present FaceKit, a computational framework for quantitative facial phenotyping from frontal facial photographs. FaceKit extracts standardized measurements of facial landmarks and derived 120 morphological features, then reports feature-level z-scores representing deviation from population reference distributions. The reference distributions are built from the FairFace dataset spanning diverse ancestral groups. We evaluated FaceKit on a curated subset of the GestaltMatcher Database covering 50 rare-disease cohorts. In addition to quantitative facial analysis, FaceKit includes synthetic facial image generation to support rare disease model development and data augmentation. We also performed privacy evaluation to assess whether synthetic images reveal identifiable information from real patient photographs and could compromise patient privacy. Across disease case studies, FaceKit-derived quantitative measurements captured known facial features associated with rare genetic disorders and provided objective support for clinical phenotyping. Together, these results establish FaceKit as a useful tool for quantitative phenotyping, and has the potential to improve rare disease diagnosis, support genotype-phenotype studies, and enable more reproducible clinical characterization across diverse patient populations.

AI.tldr: FaceKit is a computational framework for quantitative facial phenotyping from frontal photographs, providing standardized landmark measurements and z-scores against diverse reference distributions, validated across 50 rare-disease cohorts, with synthetic image generation and privacy evaluation.
AI.motivation: Rare genetic diseases have recognizable craniofacial features, but traditional facial morphology description relies on subjective, non-standardized qualitative clinical observation and free-text. HPO terms are categorical rather than quantitative and vary by examiner, limiting reproducibility across observers and institutions.
AI.method: FaceKit extracts standardized facial landmark measurements and 120 derived morphological features from frontal photographs, reporting feature-level z-scores against population reference distributions built from the FairFace dataset spanning diverse ancestral groups. It also includes synthetic facial image generation for rare disease model development and data augmentation, plus a privacy evaluation assessing whether synthetic images leak identifiable information from real patients. Evaluation used a curated subset of the GestaltMatcher Database covering 50 rare-disease cohorts.
AI.result: Across disease case studies, FaceKit-derived quantitative measurements captured known facial features associated with rare genetic disorders and provided objective support for clinical phenotyping.
AI.conclusion: FaceKit is a useful tool for quantitative phenotyping with potential to improve rare disease diagnosis, support genotype-phenotype studies, and enable more reproducible clinical characterization across diverse patient populations.

title: De novo design of monoclonal and bispecific antibodies with OFAntibody
summary: Recent advances in generative protein design have enabled de novo antibody generation with explicit target and epitope conditioning. However, most existing approaches remain formulated around a single antigen-antibody interface, whereas bispecific antibody design requires modeling multi-component complexes in which multiple target-recognition interfaces must coexist and interact within a shared antibody structure. Here we present OFAntibody, an all-atom generative framework for de novo design of monoclonal and bispecific antibodies. OFAntibody expands CDR-epitope interaction learning with large-scale distilled antigen-antibody complexes, and introduces multi-component structural supervision and arm-aware multi-hotspot routing to learn compatible multi-interface geometries and couple each antibody paratope to its designated epitope. OFAntibody supports epitope-conditioned generation across monoclonal antibodies and diverse bispecific formats, including tandem VHH, diabody and CODV. In nanobody design benchmarks, OFAntibody achieves a Top-5 enrichment rate of 41.5%, representing a 5.39-fold improvement over RFantibody in competitive candidate ranking. In bispecific antibody design tasks, OFAntibody achieves hotspot pass rates of 94-100% across the three evaluated tasks and achieves energy pass rates of 60%, 13% and 8% for diabody, tandem VHH and CODV formats, respectively. OFAntibody further enables the same target combination to be explored across different antibody formats, while joint multi-interface generation reduces geometric incompatibilities arising from independent design and post hoc assembly. Together, these results extend de novo antibody design from binary antigen-antibody complexes to programmable multi-component complexes, providing a foundation for designing single molecules that combine recognition of distinct targets and their associated biological functions.

AI.tldr: OFAntibody is an all-atom generative framework for de novo design of monoclonal and bispecific antibodies, extending CDR-epitope learning to multi-component complexes with arm-aware multi-hotspot routing.
AI.motivation: Most generative antibody design methods are formulated around a single antigen-antibody interface, but bispecific antibodies require modeling multi-component complexes where multiple target-recognition interfaces coexist and interact within a shared antibody structure.
AI.method: OFAntibody expands CDR-epitope interaction learning using large-scale distilled antigen-antibody complexes, and introduces multi-component structural supervision plus arm-aware multi-hotspot routing to learn compatible multi-interface geometries and couple each paratope to its designated epitope. It supports epitope-conditioned generation for monoclonal antibodies and bispecific formats (tandem VHH, diabody, CODV).
AI.result: In nanobody benchmarks, OFAntibody reaches 41.5% Top-5 enrichment (5.39x over RFantibody). For bispecific design, hotspot pass rates are 94-100% across three tasks, with energy pass rates of 60%, 13%, and 8% for diabody, tandem VHH, and CODV. Joint multi-interface generation reduces geometric incompatibilities from independent design and post hoc assembly.
AI.conclusion: OFAntibody extends de novo antibody design from binary antigen-antibody complexes to programmable multi-component complexes, providing a foundation for designing single molecules that combine recognition of distinct targets and their associated biological functions.

title: Connectome-Based Modeling of Mutation-Specific Amyloid-$β$ Aggregation in Familial Alzheimer's Disease
summary: Familial amyloid-$β$ (A$β$) variants alter aggregation kinetics, but their interaction with structural brain connectivity remains incompletely understood. We developed a mutation-aware mechanistic model coupling a coarse-grained monomer--oligomer--fibril aggregation--fragmentation system to graph diffusion on the 540-node Budapest Reference Connectome component. Experimental A$β_{42}$ nucleation scores scaled primary nucleation rates for seven variants relative to wild type. Robustness was examined using mutation-score uncertainty, alternative kinetic mappings, global sensitivity analysis, seed and edge-weight perturbations, degree-preserving randomized connectomes, spatial propagation analysis, synthetic ABC-SMC parameter recovery, posterior prediction, and Chemical Langevin simulations. E22G showed the earliest threshold crossing and greatest cumulative oligomer burden, whereas A2V was delayed under the selected mapping. Mutation rankings persisted across tested network perturbations, although regional burden patterns depended on topology. Connectome distance from seed regions was associated with later oligomer arrival (Spearman $ρ\approx0.92$). Under inferred parameter uncertainty, the mean timing-rank correlation was 0.990 and cumulative-burden ordering was preserved in every posterior draw, while exact peak-amplitude ordering was less stable. Stochastic ensemble medians retained the deterministic ordering despite overlap among trajectories. Within this proof-of-concept framework, mutation-dependent kinetics primarily influence aggregation timing and cumulative burden, while connectivity shapes spatial propagation. Nominal background rates, model-time units, and synthetic parameter recovery limit interpretation to mechanistic comparisons rather than clinically calibrated prediction.

AI.tldr: A mutation-aware model couples Aβ monomer-oligomer-fibril aggregation kinetics with graph diffusion on the Budapest Connectome, showing that familial mutations mainly shift aggregation timing/burden while connectivity governs spatial spread.
AI.motivation: Familial Aβ variants alter aggregation kinetics, but how these kinetic changes interact with structural brain connectivity is not well understood. The paper aims to disentangle the relative roles of mutation-driven kinetics versus network topology.
AI.method: A coarse-grained monomer–oligomer–fibril aggregation–fragmentation system was coupled to graph diffusion on the 540-node Budapest Reference Connectome. Experimental Aβ42 nucleation scores scaled primary nucleation rates for seven variants vs wild type. Robustness was tested via mutation-score uncertainty, alternative kinetic mappings, global sensitivity analysis, seed/edge perturbations, degree-preserving randomized connectomes, spatial propagation, synthetic ABC-SMC recovery, posterior prediction, and Chemical Langevin simulations.
AI.result: E22G showed earliest threshold crossing and greatest cumulative oligomer burden; A2V was delayed. Mutation rankings persisted across network perturbations, though regional burden depended on topology. Connectome distance from seed regions predicted later oligomer arrival (Spearman ρ≈0.92). Under parameter uncertainty, mean timing-rank correlation was 0.990 with cumulative-burden ordering preserved in every posterior draw; exact peak-amplitude ordering was less stable. Stochastic medians retained deterministic ordering.
AI.conclusion: In this proof-of-concept framework, mutation-dependent kinetics primarily govern aggregation timing and cumulative burden, while connectivity shapes spatial propagation. Nominal background rates, model-time units, and synthetic parameter recovery restrict interpretation to mechanistic comparisons rather than clinically calibrated prediction.

title: CircuitATLAS: Agentic reasoning over a systems neuroscience knowledge graph for target discovery in circuitopathies
summary: Drug discovery for neurological disease has traditionally centered on the molecules altered by disease. But the molecules that cause pathology are not necessarily the best points from which to reverse it. Here, we ask which otherwise unaltered molecular control points can be engaged to restore pathological neural circuits toward functional states. We present CircuitATLAS, a provenance-grounded systems-neuroscience knowledge graph and agentic framework for target discovery in circuitopathies. It structures literature-derived relationships across diseases, phenotypes, electrophysiology, circuits, brain regions, cell types and molecular effectors, while deliberately excluding direct disease-gene and disease-protein edges to reduce shortcut reasoning. The graph contains 3.83 million nodes and 7.66 million edges, including 5.31 million LLM-extracted relations, and incorporates structured datasets such as the Human Cell Atlas and new multimodal in vivo measurements. We then introduce an agentic workflow that reasons from measurable disease phenotypes through their circuit and cellular substrates to molecular interventions, therapeutic feasibility and clinical constraints. Finally, we introduce a human-governed in vivo lab-in-the-loop linking hypothesis generation to experimental iteration. Within this framework an agent nominated ATP1A3, the neuronal alpha3 Na+/K+-ATPase, as a control point on cortical excitability; interneuron-restricted expression of ATP1A3 abolished the beta- and gamma-band response to a focal 4-aminopyridine challenge in vivo, and the validated target was then carried into a structure-guided small-molecule campaign terminating in a defined assay to resolve the direction of modulation. CircuitATLAS thus provides a framework for discovering therapeutics based not only on what is molecularly disrupted in disease, but on what can be controlled to restore circuit function.

AI.tldr: CircuitATLAS is a provenance-grounded systems-neuroscience knowledge graph and agentic framework that identifies unaltered molecular control points to restore pathological neural circuits, validated by nominating ATP1A3 as a cortical excitability target.
AI.motivation: Drug discovery for neurological disease traditionally targets molecules altered by disease, but such molecules are not necessarily the best points to reverse pathology. The authors ask which otherwise unaltered molecular control points can be engaged to restore pathological neural circuits to functional states.
AI.method: CircuitATLAS integrates a knowledge graph (3.83M nodes, 7.66M edges, 5.31M LLM-extracted relations) covering diseases, phenotypes, electrophysiology, circuits, brain regions, cell types, and molecular effectors, deliberately excluding direct disease-gene/protein edges to avoid shortcut reasoning. Includes Human Cell Atlas and multimodal in vivo data. An agentic workflow reasons from measurable phenotypes through circuit/cellular substrates to molecular interventions. A human-governed in vivo lab-in-the-loop links hypothesis generation to experimental iteration.
AI.result: The agent nominated ATP1A3 (neuronal alpha3 Na+/K+-ATPase) as a control point on cortical excitability. Interneuron-restricted ATP1A3 expression abolished beta- and gamma-band response to focal 4-aminopyridine challenge in vivo. The validated target was carried into a structure-guided small-molecule campaign ending in a defined assay to resolve modulation direction.
AI.conclusion: CircuitATLAS provides a framework for discovering therapeutics based not only on what is molecularly disrupted in disease, but on what can be controlled to restore circuit function.

title: Mathematical statistics of wild mammal biomass
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, subfolder Definitions for mdpi style files
summary: Using the recently published global census of the biomass of wild terrestrial mammals, we perform a detailed mathematical statistical analysis of its distribution over $N_s=4795$ species, drawing on tools developed in economics to characterize wealth inequality. We show that the Lorenz curve of the mammal biomass distribution is characterized by a large Gini coefficient $G=0.944$ exceeding the inequality reported for wealth distribution among world countries. This distribution is compared to the predictions of the Wealth Thermalization Hypothesis (WTH), in which species biomass values are treated as energy levels populated according to a Rayleigh-Jeans (RJ) steady-state distribution. We show that an RJ extended spectral model reproduces the real Lorenz and Pareto curves over four orders of magnitude of biomass variation, capturing the strong condensation of biomass among the rare, heavy-bodied species and its near-absence among the vast majority of light-bodied ones. These results extend the WTH framework, previously validated on distributions of human economic origin, to a biological distribution shaped by ecological and evolutionary constraints, and place the extreme rarity of large-bodied mammal species within the same statistical mathematical description as the oligarchic concentration of wealth in human societies. We finally discuss possible ecological mechanisms that may contribute to the observed distribution, including interspecific interactions, food availability, and competition.

AI.tldr: The paper applies economic inequality metrics (Lorenz curve, Gini) to the global biomass distribution of 4795 wild terrestrial mammal species, finding extreme inequality (G=0.944). It shows an extended Rayleigh-Jeans spectral model from the Wealth Thermalization Hypothesis reproduces the observed Lorenz and Pareto curves across four orders of magnitude.
AI.motivation: Recent availability of a global census of wild terrestrial mammal biomass enables quantitative analysis. The authors aim to test whether tools from economics (wealth inequality) and the Wealth Thermalization Hypothesis—previously validated on human economic distributions—also describe a biological distribution shaped by ecological and evolutionary constraints.
AI.method: Mathematical statistical analysis of biomass across N_s = 4795 species using Lorenz curves and Gini coefficients; comparison with the Wealth Thermalization Hypothesis (WTH), modeling species biomass as energy levels following a Rayleigh-Jeans (RJ) steady-state distribution via an extended spectral model.
AI.result: The biomass distribution has a Gini coefficient G = 0.944, exceeding wealth inequality among world countries. The RJ extended spectral model reproduces real Lorenz and Pareto curves over four orders of magnitude of biomass variation, capturing strong biomass condensation among rare heavy-bodied species and near-absence among light-bodied ones.
AI.conclusion: The WTH framework extends beyond human economic distributions to a biological distribution governed by ecological/evolutionary constraints, linking extreme rarity of large-bodied mammals to oligarchic wealth concentration. The authors discuss ecological mechanisms possibly underlying the pattern, including interspecific interactions, food availability, and competition.

title: Feedback to the primary visual cortex is highly concentrated on the central visual field representation
comment: 24 pages, 3 figures (2 figures in the main text, 1 figure in supplementary material)
summary: Retrograde tracer injections in marmoset monkeys revealed a striking feature of neural circuitry in primate visual system: among neurons projecting to the primary visual cortex (striate cortex, V1), the proportion of extrastriate feedback neurons relative to thalamic feedforward neurons decreases markedly with visual field eccentricity. This supports the Central-Peripheral Dichotomy theory, which proposes fundamentally distinct computational specializations --- visual recognition and attentional selection, respectively --- in the central and peripheral visual fields.

AI.tldr: Retrograde tracing in marmosets shows the ratio of extrastriate feedback to thalamic feedforward inputs to V1 declines with visual field eccentricity, supporting the Central-Peripheral Dichotomy theory.
AI.motivation: To test the Central-Peripheral Dichotomy theory, which posits distinct computational roles for central (visual recognition) versus peripheral (attentional selection) visual fields, by examining whether the balance of feedback versus feedforward circuitry to V1 varies with eccentricity.
AI.method: Retrograde tracer injections into marmoset monkeys to quantify neurons projecting to V1, comparing extrastriate feedback neurons against thalamic feedforward neurons across visual field eccentricities.
AI.result: The proportion of extrastriate feedback neurons relative to thalamic feedforward neurons projecting to V1 decreases markedly with increasing visual field eccentricity.
AI.conclusion: The eccentricity-dependent shift in feedback-to-feedforward balance in primate visual circuitry supports the Central-Peripheral Dichotomy theory.

title: Structure alone supports efficient visual computation in the Drosophila visual system
summary: Understanding the extent to which measured synaptic wiring determines computation remains a central challenge. Here, we couple the proofread adult Drosophila melanogaster connectome to an anatomically faithful model of its eye. Visual information is inputted in the eye model, then passed to the connectome, and finally read from a Kenyon-cell-centered linear decoder. This creates a connectome-only model in which the anatomical graph and eye geometry are fixed and only scalar synaptic gains and neuronal thresholds may be learned. The model supports multitask vision, including color discrimination, shape classification, and numerical discrimination that follows a ratio-dependent scaling characteristic of approximate number perception. To test whether precise connectivity is consequential under wiring economy, we compare the biological graph to randomized ensembles that increasingly preserve biological synaptic constraints. At matched wiring cost, the biological network consistently yields higher accuracy, whereas less constrained rewiring surpasses it at the cost of inflated wiring. These findings indicate that the measured connectivity and eye geometry jointly set efficient operating points for visual computation.

AI.tldr: The adult Drosophila connectome coupled with an anatomically faithful eye model performs multitask vision at matched wiring cost better than randomized networks, showing that measured connectivity and eye geometry set efficient computational operating points.
AI.motivation: A central challenge is understanding how much measured synaptic wiring determines computation. The authors test whether precise biological connectivity is consequential for visual computation under wiring economy constraints.
AI.method: They couple the proofread adult Drosophila melanogaster connectome to an anatomically faithful eye model, feeding visual input through the eye to the connectome and decoding from a Kenyon-cell-centered linear decoder. Only scalar synaptic gains and neuronal thresholds are learnable; the anatomical graph and eye geometry are fixed. They compare the biological graph against randomized ensembles that increasingly preserve biological synaptic constraints.
AI.result: The model supports multitask vision, including color discrimination, shape classification, and numerical discrimination showing ratio-dependent scaling characteristic of approximate number perception. At matched wiring cost, the biological network consistently yields higher accuracy, while less constrained rewiring only surpasses it with inflated wiring cost.
AI.conclusion: The measured connectivity and eye geometry jointly set efficient operating points for visual computation.

title: Truecell reproduces R Seurat's single-cell analysis outputs natively in the Python ecosystem
summary: Single-cell RNA-sequencing analyses predominantly use either Seurat (R) or Scanpy (Python), with the choice often driven by programming language preference. However, by default, these tools produce divergent variable features, neighbour graphs, clusters, and marker genes. Laboratories requiring Python, which supports most deep-learning, foundation-model, and agent tools, must re-implement Seurat analyses in a framework that does not replicate Seurat's results. Truecell was developed as a Python implementation of the Seurat interface, preserving function names, arguments, default settings, and the object model to facilitate seamless transfer of analyses. In eighteen paired end-to-end evaluations against R Seurat, deterministic outputs matched to floating-point precision, and fold-change order was identical across all nine differential expression tests. In a three-arm benchmark on three datasets, with fixed user parameters and 20 seeds per tool, Truecell more closely reproduced Seurat's clustering than a Seurat-configured Scanpy in all 12 combinations of dataset and resolution settings. Truecell's marker genes and enriched pathways were also closer to Seurat's than Scanpy's were, and pseudobulk DESeq2 reproduced Seurat's gene lists with a Jaccard index ranging from 0.95 to 1.00. This agreement reflects fidelity to Seurat rather than biological correctness.

AI.tldr: Truecell is a Python re-implementation of the Seurat single-cell RNA-seq interface that reproduces Seurat outputs to floating-point precision, outperforming Scanpy in matching Seurat's clusters, marker genes, and pathways.
AI.motivation: Seurat (R) and Scanpy (Python) produce divergent variable features, neighbour graphs, clusters, and marker genes by default. Labs needing Python (for deep-learning, foundation models, agent tools) must re-implement Seurat analyses in a framework that does not replicate Seurat's results, creating cross-language inconsistency.
AI.method: Developed Truecell as a Python implementation of the Seurat interface, preserving function names, arguments, default settings, and the object model for seamless analysis transfer. Evaluated via eighteen paired end-to-end comparisons against R Seurat, a three-arm benchmark on three datasets (fixed parameters, 20 seeds per tool) comparing against a Seurat-configured Scanpy, and pseudobulk DESeq2 marker gene comparisons.
AI.result: Deterministic outputs matched Seurat to floating-point precision across 18 paired evaluations; fold-change order identical in all nine differential expression tests. Truecell more closely reproduced Seurat's clustering than Seurat-configured Scanpy in all 12 dataset/resolution combinations. Truecell's marker genes and enriched pathways were closer to Seurat's than Scanpy's, and pseudobulk DESeq2 reproduced Seurat's gene lists with Jaccard index 0.95–1.00.
AI.conclusion: Truecell achieves high fidelity to Seurat, enabling Python-based workflows without loss of compatibility. The authors note this agreement reflects fidelity to Seurat rather than biological correctness.

title: Stochasticity and Environmental Switching Shape Quorum Sensing Evolution in Bacterial Populations
summary: Quorum sensing (QS) is classically understood as a mechanism by which bacterial cells sense their own density, but environmental fluctuations make any single cell's estimate unreliable. An alternative view holds that populations pool individual estimates to reach reliable collective decisions. We investigate how a two-autoinducer toggle switch network enables this collective adaptation in fluctuating environments. At the single-cell level, the toggle switch is bistable. Membrane permeability controls autoinducer secretion and is the evolving trait. Using an individual-based model of a spatially structured population, we show that permeability evolves through a collective mechanism. Environmental frequency is the primary determinant of evolutionary outcome. Under strong asymmetry, the dominant trait reaches a high plateau. The trait linked to the rare environment stays low. It rises smoothly as its environment becomes more frequent. Total permeability stays close to a fixed budget; environmental frequency mainly sets how it is split between the two traits. When the two environments are equally frequent, no single trait wins. Both traits coexist, and noise asymmetry between the two sensing channels biases the levels at which they coexist rather than selecting a winner. Coexistence is also the slowest outcome to reach. Higher noise speeds adaptation, but the evolved permeability is non-monotonic in noise, peaking at an intermediate value. Earlier work found that more noise favors collective sensing as long as cells are correct on average. We develop a two-trait adaptive-dynamics model that unifies these regimes. Away from symmetry, it reduces to a closed one-dimensional equation that captures the individual-based results. At symmetry, weak cross-repression gives a single coexistence attractor, consistent with replicate populations maintaining both traits.

AI.tldr: A two-autoinducer toggle switch enables bacterial populations to pool noisy individual estimates for collective sensing; membrane permeability evolves so that total sensing budget stays fixed while environmental frequency splits it between two traits.
AI.motivation: Quorum sensing is classically seen as single cells sensing their own density, but environmental fluctuations make individual estimates unreliable. An alternative view is that populations pool individual estimates to make reliable collective decisions, and it is unclear how network structure enables this collective adaptation.
AI.method: An individual-based model of a spatially structured population where membrane permeability (an evolving trait) controls autoinducer secretion in a bistable two-autoinducer toggle switch. A complementary two-trait adaptive-dynamics model is developed to unify regimes.
AI.result: Environmental frequency primarily determines evolutionary outcome. Under strong asymmetry the dominant trait plateaus high while the rare-environment trait stays low; total permeability stays near a fixed budget, and frequency mainly sets how it is split. At equal frequencies, both traits coexist (no winner), with noise asymmetry between channels biasing coexistence levels. Coexistence is slowest. Higher noise speeds adaptation, but evolved permeability peaks at intermediate noise.
AI.conclusion: The two-trait adaptive-dynamics model unifies previously separate noise regimes: away from symmetry it reduces to a closed 1D equation matching the individual-based results, and at symmetry weak cross-repression yields a single coexistence attractor consistent with replicate populations maintaining both traits.

title: A Connectome Test of the Fly Hashing Algorithm
comment: 7 pages, 5 figures. Code, data pipeline and results: https://github.com/ssenge/FlyHash-Connectome
summary: Dasgupta, Stevens and Navlakha (2017) showed that the Drosophila olfactory circuit, modelled as a random sparse projection followed by winner-take-all, is a locality-sensitive hash that beats classical LSH. The projection was random because the wiring was unknown. We test it against four electron-microscopy connectomes (MaleCNS, hemibrain, FlyWire, BANC; four animals, seven hemispheres). First, the 2017 pattern holds in a reimplementation of its protocol on SIFT, MNIST and odour mixtures (GloVe is near chance at short codes for every method): the fly hash beats k Gaussian projections at short hash lengths (3.1x in AP@200 on MNIST at k = 4). Second, against the tested real-valued Gaussian baseline that advantage is per active cell, not per operation: Gaussian projections given the same projection arithmetic retrieve better on every dataset and input dimension tested. Third, across four connectomes the measured pairing of glomeruli gives no consistent retrieval advantage over degree-preserving rewiring: retrieval is slightly lower (median -1.6%), and the small odour deficits depend on how missing odour responses are treated. Separately, equalising glomerular fan-out at fixed connection count improves retrieval in the model in every hemisphere, while equalising inputs per cell lowers it on average. Yet the fan-out profile is similar across the four sampled animals (median between-animal Spearman rho = 0.86), structural synapse counts do not offset it, and its relation to odour tuning is weak. In the model that uneven allocation costs retrieval. For practice: measured wiring gives no consistent retrieval advantage over degree-preserving random wiring, so a fly hash needs no connectome data, and its advantage is per active unit, which may suit hardware where active units rather than arithmetic are the binding cost, a hypothesis we do not test.

AI.tldr: The Drosophila olfactory circuit as an LSH is re-examined across four EM connectomes: the fly hash's advantage holds per active cell but not per operation, and measured wiring gives no consistent retrieval advantage over degree-preserving random rewiring.
AI.motivation: The 2017 claim that the fly olfactory circuit (random sparse projection + winner-take-all) beats classical LSH rested on an assumed random wiring because the true connectome was unknown. This work tests whether real, measured wiring provides any retrieval advantage over the random model, and clarifies the true nature of the fly hash's advantage.
AI.method: Reimplements the 2017 protocol on SIFT, MNIST, and odour mixtures (plus GloVe), comparing the fly hash against k Gaussian projections at various hash lengths. Then tests four EM connectomes (MaleCNS, hemibrain, FlyWire, BANC; four animals, seven hemispheres) against degree-preserving rewiring, and separately perturbs glomerular fan-out and inputs-per-cell to probe allocation effects.
AI.result: The 2017 pattern reproduces (fly hash beats k Gaussian projections at short codes, e.g. 3.1x AP@200 on MNIST at k=4). However, against a real-valued Gaussian baseline the advantage is per active cell, not per operation—Gaussians retrieve better on every dataset/dimension tested. Measured glomeruli pairing yields no consistent advantage over degree-preserving rewiring (median -1.6% retrieval). Equalising fan-out improves retrieval in every hemisphere; equalising inputs per cell lowers it. Fan-out profile is consistent across animals (median Spearman rho = 0.86), but structural synapse counts and odour tuning relate only weakly.
AI.conclusion: Measured wiring offers no consistent retrieval advantage over degree-preserving random wiring, so a fly hash needs no connectome data. Its advantage is per active unit rather than per arithmetic operation, which may suit hardware where active units are the binding cost (an untested hypothesis).

title: MovieSTAGE: Scene, Transition, and Global Encoding for Movie-fMRI ADHD Classification
comment: Accepted to the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Bioinformatics and Biomedicine (BIBM 2026)
summary: Naturalistic movie-fMRI provides a shared, temporally structured probe of brain dynamics, yet predictive models commonly rely on whole-run functional connectivity (FC) or temporally generic representations that are not aligned with narrative events. We introduce MovieSTAGE (Scene, Transition, and Global Encoding), a multiscale framework that combines hypergraph-structured FC-profile organization within scenes, unsigned FC-profile differences across adjacent scenes, and whole-movie FC. We evaluated 260 participants from the CMI-HBN Despicable Me cohort on case-control, ADHD-subtype, and three-class classification using 10 repetitions of stratified five-fold cross-validation, complete out-of-fold (OOF) predictions, and paired subject-cluster bootstrap and permutation tests. MovieSTAGE achieved AUROCs of 0.69, 0.73, and 0.75 and balanced accuracies of 67.6%, 69.8%, and 58.3%, respectively, yielding the highest mean point estimates among the evaluated methods. On the three-class task, the full model outperformed all two-branch variants, the HGNN scene encoder outperformed MLP, GAT, and BNT alternatives under matched settings, and the human-annotated partition outperformed duration-matched random and fixed-count GSBS controls. These controlled results support incremental predictive value from event-aligned scene and transition representations when combined with whole-movie FC in this cohort. Post-hoc model-derived analyses generated network-level hypotheses involving frontoparietal and default-mode systems.

AI.tldr: MovieSTAGE, a multiscale movie-fMRI framework combining scene-level hypergraph FC, cross-scene FC transitions, and whole-movie FC, improves classification of ADHD case-control, subtype, and three-class outcomes in the CMI-HBN cohort.
AI.motivation: Movie-fMRI offers a shared, temporally structured probe of brain dynamics, but predictive models typically use whole-run functional connectivity or temporally generic representations that ignore narrative event alignment.
AI.method: MovieSTAGE (Scene, Transition, Global Encoding) organizes hypergraph-structured FC profiles within scenes, unsigned FC-profile differences across adjacent scenes, and whole-movie FC. Evaluated on 260 CMI-HBN Despicable Me participants using 10 repetitions of stratified 5-fold CV, complete out-of-fold predictions, and paired subject-cluster bootstrap/permutation tests, with ablations against two-branch variants, HGNN vs. MLP/GAT/BNT encoders, and human vs. random/fixed-count GSBS partitions.
AI.result: AUROCs of 0.69, 0.73, and 0.75 and balanced accuracies of 67.6%, 69.8%, and 58.3% for case-control, subtype, and three-class tasks, respectively; highest mean point estimates among evaluated methods. Full model beat all two-branch variants; HGNN scene encoder beat MLP, GAT, and BNT; human-annotated partition beat controls.
AI.conclusion: Event-aligned scene and transition representations add incremental predictive value beyond whole-movie FC in this cohort. Post-hoc analyses suggest network-level hypotheses involving frontoparietal and default-mode systems.

title: Many Brains, One Geometry: A Shared Visual-Semantic Space for Cross-Dataset fMRI Decoding
comment: 21 pages, 5 figures, 1 table, 3 supplementary figures, 2 supplementary tables
summary: Visual decoding from fMRI is typically siloed by participant and experiment, obscuring whether heterogeneous neural measurements can be organized within a common computational geometry. Here we introduce BRAID-fMRI (Brain Representation Alignment across Individuals and Datasets), a shared CLIP-supervised decoding framework. BRAID-fMRI uses a single ROI-wise Transformer with optional participant conditioning across eight visual-fMRI datasets comprising 93 dataset-specific participant entries, 430,007 single-trial responses and 162,839 unique stimuli. Regional brain activity is aligned with 512-dimensional CLIP ViT-B/32 representations using a multi-positive contrastive objective that treats repeated stimuli across participants and datasets as positives. BRAID-fMRI supports retrieval across seven evaluation datasets. On eight matched participant entries, it achieves 35.0 +/- 11.1% Top-10 accuracy, exceeding the observed mean accuracy of the two evaluated baselines - the MindEye-style pooled-CLIP decoder (27.1 +/- 5.1%) and ridge regression (21.1 +/- 9.1%) - and attaining the highest observed accuracy for seven of eight entries. In separately trained participant-agnostic models, expanding the source pool increased target-dataset holdout accuracy by up to 92.1% relative to the initial source-training condition. The learned space preserves graded semantic structure, while ablations and saliency highlight ventral and early visual cortex and category-specific motion and attentional systems. These results support scalable cross-dataset decoding into a common CLIP-aligned space, with model sensitivity concentrated in ventral and early visual inputs.

AI.tldr: BRAID-fMRI is a shared CLIP-supervised Transformer framework that aligns fMRI brain activity across participants and datasets into a common decoding space, outperforming baseline decoders and scaling with more source data.
AI.motivation: Visual decoding from fMRI is usually siloed by participant and experiment, making it unclear whether heterogeneous neural measurements can be organized within a common computational geometry.
AI.method: BRAID-fMRI (Brain Representation Alignment across Individuals and Datasets) uses a single ROI-wise Transformer with optional participant conditioning, trained on eight visual-fMRI datasets (93 participant entries, 430,007 trials, 162,839 stimuli). It aligns regional brain activity to 512-dim CLIP ViT-B/32 representations via a multi-positive contrastive objective treating repeated stimuli across participants/datasets as positives.
AI.result: On eight matched entries, BRAID-fMRI reaches 35.0 +/- 11.1% Top-10 accuracy, beating MindEye-style pooled-CLIP (27.1 +/- 5.1%) and ridge regression (21.1 +/- 9.1%), with best accuracy on 7/8. Participant-agnostic models improved holdout accuracy up to 92.1% with more source data. The space preserves graded semantic structure; saliency highlights ventral/early visual cortex and category-specific motion/attentional systems.
AI.conclusion: Results support scalable cross-dataset decoding into a common CLIP-aligned space, with model sensitivity concentrated in ventral and early visual inputs.

title: Predicting Long-Term ADAS-Cog Change From Early Response After Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation in Alzheimer Disease
summary: Early cognitive response after repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) may predict later cognitive change in Alzheimer disease, but the incremental value of domain-specific response is unclear. We analyzed data from 112 randomized participants; 101 entered a Week-5 landmark cohort and 91 had complete predictors and outcomes at 8, 16, and 24 weeks post-treatment. Nested predictor-set comparisons used ridge regression to evaluate baseline information, trial variables, early total-score response, and domain-specific response. Model-class comparisons included ridge, multi-task elastic net, restricted random forest, and longitudinal mixed effects. Validation used repeated treatment-site-stratified 5-fold cross-validation with five repetitions, nested hyperparameter tuning, and paired participant-level bootstrap comparisons with 10,000 resamples. Adding Week-3 and Week-5 ADAS-Cog total-score response improved prediction. The early total-response ridge achieved overall MAE 3.067, RMSE 3.885, and $R^2=0.384$. Replacing two total-response variables with 22 component-level changes worsened performance (MAE 3.363, RMSE 4.269, $R^2=0.257$). The paired MAE difference was -0.297 points (95% CI -0.485 to -0.115). Mixed effects was competitive (MAE 3.162), with an uncertain overall difference from total-response ridge. Sensitivity analyses using absolute future scores and excluding Week-3 response supported the main findings. In this sample, early aggregate ADAS-Cog response was more informative than a higher-dimensional domain-specific representation. The model is an internally validated early-response updating tool, not a pretreatment selection model or evidence of causal rTMS efficacy.

AI.tldr: Early total-score ADAS-Cog response after rTMS predicts later cognitive change in AD better than domain-specific response; an internally validated ridge model shows aggregate response is more informative.
AI.motivation: Early cognitive response after rTMS may predict later cognitive change in Alzheimer disease, but whether domain-specific response adds incremental predictive value over total-score response is unclear.
AI.method: Analyzed 112 randomized participants (101 in Week-5 landmark cohort; 91 with complete data at 8/16/24 weeks). Used nested predictor-set comparisons with ridge regression to evaluate baseline info, trial variables, early total-score response, and domain-specific response. Compared model classes: ridge, multi-task elastic net, restricted random forest, and longitudinal mixed effects. Validation via repeated treatment-site-stratified 5-fold CV (5 reps), nested hyperparameter tuning, and paired participant-level bootstrap (10,000 resamples).
AI.result: Adding Week-3 and Week-5 ADAS-Cog total-score response improved prediction (total-response ridge: MAE 3.067, RMSE 3.885, R²=0.384). Replacing two total-response variables with 22 component-level changes worsened performance (MAE 3.363, RMSE 4.269, R²=0.257; paired MAE difference -0.297, 95% CI -0.485 to -0.115). Mixed effects was competitive (MAE 3.162) with uncertain overall difference. Sensitivity analyses supported findings.
AI.conclusion: Early aggregate ADAS-Cog response was more informative than a higher-dimensional domain-specific representation. The model is an internally validated early-response updating tool, not a pretreatment selection model or evidence of causal rTMS efficacy.

title: Do Generative Priors Align with Human Naturalness Perception?
summary: Visual generative models are trained to capture the probability distributions of natural images, yet whether their native priors reflect the regularities governing human perception of image naturalness remains an open question. Here, we probe these priors through native prediction errors across 25 open image and video generators. Because raw single-image losses are dominated by scene content and visual complexity, we evaluate directional loss differences using content-preserving, paired relational interventions that selectively disrupt facial configurations or physical illumination consistency while limiting changes in low-level image statistics. Across both domains, these loss differences reproduce human-like selective sensitivities and tolerances, capturing the classic Thatcher effect on faces and shape-dependent responses to illumination inconsistencies. Notably, these loss differences reliably track continuous gradations of human naturalness judgments across individual stimulus pairs (peaking at $r = .84$ on faces and $.64$ on physical scenes) and retain unique human-aligned signals even after controlling for feature distances from frozen vision encoders and standard image quality metrics. We also find that while overall sensitivity to these violations broadly covaries with human alignment across models, the two systematically decouple along denoising schedules, with alignment peaking earlier than sensitivity, revealing that human-like naturalness judgments dissociate from generic violation detection. Together, these findings demonstrate that learning visual distributions yields generative loss landscapes that capture distinct aspects of human naturalness perception.

AI.tldr: Native prediction errors of 25 visual generators reproduce human naturalness perception, including the Thatcher effect and illumination sensitivities, decoupling alignment from violation sensitivity along denoising schedules.
AI.motivation: Whether generative models' learned priors reflect the regularities governing human perception of image naturalness is an open question. Raw single-image losses are confounded by scene content and visual complexity, making direct comparison difficult.
AI.method: Using content-preserving paired relational interventions that selectively disrupt facial configurations or physical illumination consistency while limiting changes in low-level image statistics, the authors probe native prediction errors across 25 open image and video generators, comparing directional loss differences to human judgments.
AI.result: Loss differences reproduce human-like selective sensitivities and tolerances (Thatcher effect; shape-dependent illumination responses), track continuous gradations of human naturalness judgments (r = .84 faces, .64 physical scenes), and retain unique human-aligned signals beyond frozen vision encoders and standard image quality metrics. Sensitivity covaries with human alignment across models but decouples along denoising schedules, with alignment peaking earlier.
AI.conclusion: Learning visual distributions yields generative loss landscapes capturing distinct aspects of human naturalness perception; human-like naturalness judgments dissociate from generic violation detection.

title: Label-free cell counting and viability prediction with brightfield imaging and deep learning
summary: Cell viability assessment is a core requirement in cell culture systems, with critical applications in biopharmaceutical manufacturing and drug development. Conventionally, it is measured by adding membrane-impermeable dyes to a sample (a process called staining), which allows compromised cell membranes to be distinguished from intact ones. However, staining has several limitations: (a) chemical agents can perturb normal cellular processes of the cells being measured, (b) it is often ambiguous to assign viability to individual cells whose membrane integrity is only partially compromised. (c) photobleaching can undermine measurement accuracy over time when using fluorescent stains, and (d) staining cannot be performed in situ or in real time. Here, we show that (1) stained cells captured under brightfield imaging contain sufficient information to distinguish live and dead cells, and (2) cells captured under unstained brightfield imaging exhibit similar image features to their stained counterparts, enabling models trained on stained cells to generalize to unstained ones. We then report the development and validation of ViabiLens, an AI-assisted software for label-free cell viability analysis. The ViabiLens combines a cell detection model for localizing individual cells with a convolutional neural network (CNN) classifier for live/dead prediction, paired with an interactive UMAP-based viewer for visualizing and exploring individual cells across the sample. Evaluated on Chinese Hamster Ovary (CHO) cells spanning a wide range of viability conditions, ViabiLens achieves a mean absolute error of 2.68\% on unstained samples against fluorescence-based reference measurements. We also release a benchmark dataset for label-free cell viability analysis to facilitate future research, available at https://amirrezavazifeh.github.io/ViabiLens-Project-Page/.

AI.tldr: The paper presents ViabiLens, an AI-assisted, label-free software for cell viability analysis that detects and classifies live/dead cells from unstained brightfield images, achieving 2.68% mean absolute error on CHO cells.
AI.motivation: Conventional viability assessment relies on staining with membrane-impermeable dyes, which has drawbacks: chemical perturbation of cells, ambiguous viability assignment for partially compromised membranes, photobleaching of fluorescent stains, and inability to operate in situ or in real time.
AI.method: The authors show that stained brightfield images contain sufficient cues to distinguish live/dead cells and that unstained cells share similar features, allowing models trained on stained cells to generalize. ViabiLens combines a cell detection model for localization, a CNN classifier for live/dead prediction, and an interactive UMAP-based viewer for exploring individual cells.
AI.result: Evaluated on CHO cells across a wide range of viability conditions, ViabiLens achieves a mean absolute error of 2.68% on unstained samples relative to fluorescence-based reference measurements. A benchmark dataset is also released.
AI.conclusion: ViabiLens enables accurate, label-free, in situ cell viability analysis, overcoming staining limitations, with a public benchmark dataset to support future research.

title: Taxonomic Classification with Complete Tag Arrays
comment: Preliminary version: The ideas in this paper are the authors'; the code, the experiments and the text were developed by Claude Opus 5.5, an AI model by Anthropic, under their direction. We are in the process of verifying the results, including running a comparison with Cliffy, which we cannot build on the commodity machine we are currently using
summary: Taxonomic classifiers such as Kraken assign each $k$-mer of a reference database to the lowest common ancestor (LCA) of the genomes containing it, but this works less well as databases grow, because more and more $k$-mers are shared across species. Cliffy (Ahmed, Boucher and Langmead, 2025) instead uses variable-length exact matches found with an r-index, and can list approximately the genera containing each match; on 16S rRNA it is more accurate than Kraken~2, but its index is large and expensive to build. We present KATKA, which finds the maximal exact matches (MEMs) of at least a given length in each read with Boyer--Moore--Li on a run-length compressed suffix array, counts the occurrences of each MEM in each genus exactly with a complete, run-length compressed tag array, and gives each genus credit in proportion to those counts. On the SILVA 16S rRNA database, KATKA's default index takes 1.44\,GB and can be built in minutes on a desktop computer; it classifies a read in 66\,$μ$s with one thread and reaches 93.8\% genus-level accuracy, close to what Cliffy reports for its 9\,GB index. Grammar-compressing the runs of the tag array shrinks the index to 1.04\,GB, at 75\,$μ$s per read. On the same machine and reads, it is more accurate than Kraken~2 (79.3\%) and Tagger (81.7 to 92.8\%, depending on how mates that disagree are scored). Indexing minimizer digests instead of the sequences makes the index three times smaller and classification 1.7 times faster, at a cost of 1.3 points of accuracy. KATKA is available at https://github.com/TravisGagie/KATKA.

AI.tldr: KATKA is a taxonomic classifier that uses maximal exact matches found on a run-length compressed suffix array with a run-length compressed tag array to assign genus-level labels, achieving high accuracy at a much smaller index size than Cliffy.
AI.motivation: Taxonomic classifiers like Kraken degrade as databases grow because more k-mers are shared across species. Cliffy improves accuracy using variable-length exact matches with an r-index, but its index is large and expensive to build. KATKA aims to match Cliffy's accuracy with a much smaller, quickly built index.
AI.method: KATKA finds maximal exact matches (MEMs) of at least a given length in each read using Boyer-Moore-Li on a run-length compressed suffix array, counts each MEM's occurrences per genus exactly with a complete run-length compressed tag array, and credits each genus proportionally to those counts. It can also grammar-compress the tag array runs and index minimizer digests instead of full sequences.
AI.result: On SILVA 16S rRNA, KATKA's default index is 1.44 GB and builds in minutes on a desktop; it classifies a read in 66 µs single-threaded with 93.8% genus-level accuracy (close to Cliffy's 9 GB index). Grammar compression shrinks the index to 1.04 GB at 75 µs/read. It beats Kraken 2 (79.3%) and Tagger (81.7-92.8%). Indexing minimizer digests makes it 3x smaller and 1.7x faster, losing 1.3 accuracy points.
AI.conclusion: KATKA achieves accuracy comparable to Cliffy while using a far smaller index (1.44 GB vs 9 GB) that can be built in minutes, and it outperforms Kraken 2 and Tagger. It offers flexible trade-offs via grammar compression or minimizer-digest indexing. The tool is open-source at https://github.com/TravisGagie/KATKA.
